strengths: Identifies a novel and interesting failure mode ('sink trap') in native text-to-3D generative models, where text-conditioned generation collapses to near-identical geometries for out-of-distribution prompts, and provides a clear diversity-ratio metric and velocity-norm analysis to characterize it.

The proposed solution (Euler inversion with an empty/null prompt combined with null-text optimization of unconditional embeddings) is simple, well-motivated, and effective, decoupling the model's geometric representational capacity from its text-conditioning sensitivity.

To the authors' knowledge, this is the first method to enable high-fidelity, purely text-driven 3D shape editing using only a native 3D generative model, without auxiliary 2D priors, masks, or inpainting models.

Reasonably thorough empirical validation: quantitative comparisons (L1, LPIPS, SigLIP) against relevant baselines (native TRELLIS editing, VoxHammer), qualitative figures across diverse non-rigid shapes (DT4D) and generated assets, and an interesting cross-check with image-domain diffusion models (Stable Diffusion, FLUX) to contrast 3D vs 2D inversion behavior.

Practical benefits are demonstrated, including large speedup (about 20x) and improved structural fidelity/plausibility relative to the VoxHammer baseline, plus multiview-consistency verification of edits.
Honest and specific limitations section identifying failure cases (rare/out-of-distribution poses) rather than overclaiming universal robustness.
weaknesses: The entire study is conducted on a single 3D generative backbone (TRELLIS), explicitly excluding its newer iteration; it remains unclear whether the sink-trap phenomenon and the proposed fix generalize to other text-to-3D architectures or latent representations.

No human/user study is included to assess perceptual quality or semantic correctness of edits; the primary editing metric (SigLIP alignment) is a proxy that may not fully capture geometric plausibility or fidelity, especially given the qualitative failure cases shown in the limitations (Fig. 9).

Reported quantitative results (e.g., Table 2 and Table 4 L1/LPIPS values) often carry very large standard deviations relative to the means, raising questions about the statistical robustness and consistency of the improvements across samples.

Comparisons for the editing evaluation are limited to two baselines (native TRELLIS second-stage refinement and VoxHammer); other recently cited 3D-editing approaches from the related work (e.g., SDS-based, multiview-consistent, or masked-latent methods) are not directly benchmarked, making the relative standing of the method less complete.
The dataset used for editing evaluation (13 selected DT4D sequences, 16 frames each) is relatively small and hand-curated, which may limit the generality of the editing conclusions.

The method offers no explicit mechanism to enforce geometric plausibility during large semantic edits, and the paper acknowledges failures on rare poses without proposing a mitigation beyond future-work suggestions (e.g., automatic OOD detection), leaving an important robustness gap unaddressed within the current submission.
Key hyperparameters (CFG scale of 5, 50 sampling steps, 10 inner NTI optimization steps) are fixed without ablation, so sensitivity of the proposed pipeline to these choices is not analyzed.

strengths: Identifies and clearly illustrates an interesting failure mode ('sink trap') in text-to-3D flow models, where diverse out-of-distribution prompts collapse to near-identical geometries despite the model's latent space being able to represent more diverse shapes.

The proposed diagnostic metrics (diversity ratio R via SigLIP embeddings, velocity-norm analysis during inversion) provide a reasonable, interpretable way to characterize the phenomenon and distinguish 3D from 2D (T2I) model behavior.

The practical fix—inverting with an empty/null prompt plus null-text optimization instead of an approximate source prompt—is simple, well-motivated by the velocity-norm/trajectory-instability analysis, and is shown to substantially improve reconstruction fidelity over standard Euler/NTI inversion with approximate prompts.

Reasonably thorough ablations and qualitative figures (Figs. 2, 6, 7, 9-14) covering a variety of character/animal shapes, plus an honest limitations section acknowledging failure cases on geometrically out-of-distribution poses (Fig. 9).

Comparison against two relevant baselines (native TRELLIS second-stage edit and VoxHammer) with reported efficiency gains (~20x speedup over VoxHammer) and qualitative superiority in geometry retargeting.
weaknesses: All core 3D experiments are conducted on a single text-to-3D backbone (TRELLIS). The central claims about 'state-of-the-art native text-to-3D generative models' and the generality of the sink-trap phenomenon are therefore only demonstrated for one architecture; it remains unclear whether this is a general property of 3D generative models or an artifact specific to TRELLIS's structured-latent design.

The technical contribution is largely a straightforward re-application of existing Null-Text Inversion (Mokady et al.) with an empty/null source prompt rather than an approximate prompt, applied to a new domain. The algorithmic novelty is therefore modest; the main contribution is empirical/diagnostic rather than methodological.

Quantitative evaluation of the editing results is thin: Table 3 reports a single SigLIP alignment number per method with no variance, no user study, and no measures of identity/pose preservation or geometric consistency beyond qualitative figures. This is insufficient evidence to robustly support the editing-quality claims.

The diversity-ratio study (Table 1) is based on only 7 hand-picked subject categories, which is too small a sample to convincingly establish systematic 'sink trap' regions across the prompt distribution.

Table 2 results for image-based baselines (SD, FLUX) are not as uniformly 'insensitive to prompt type' as the text claims—e.g., FLUX PSNR with true vs. empty prompt (10.32 vs 16.12) varies substantially—which weakens the contrast the paper draws between 2D and 3D model robustness.
VoxHammer's reported 67% failure rate on DT4D raises concerns about whether the baseline was adequately adapted/tuned for this out-of-distribution dataset, making the comparison potentially unfair.

The method still requires per-shape/per-edit test-time optimization (NTI with Adam, 10 inner iterations over 50 timesteps), which, while faster than VoxHammer, is not an automatic or free editing solution and its sensitivity to hyperparameters is not studied.

The paper's own limitation example (Fig. 9) shows the method fails on 'geometrically out-of-distribution' poses, i.e., precisely the setting the paper is designed to address, suggesting the approach does not fully resolve the stated problem but only shifts the boundary of failure.

strengths: Identifies and clearly characterizes a novel and practically important failure mode ('sink trap') in native text-to-3D generative models, where text conditioning becomes insensitive to out-of-distribution prompts while the model retains rich geometric expressivity -- a useful diagnostic contribution for the 3D generative modeling community.

The proposed fix is simple, well-motivated, and elegant: perform inversion with an empty/null prompt plus null-text optimization to stabilize sampling trajectories, then edit purely by resampling with the target text embedding, without any auxiliary masks, multi-view 2D priors, or image inpainting models, unlike prior 3D editing pipelines.

Solid supporting analysis: SigLIP-based diversity ratio study (Table 1, Fig. 2) quantifying non-uniform semantic coverage, and velocity-norm/L1 reconstruction studies (Table 2, Fig. 4, Fig. 6) that convincingly show approximate prompts destabilize inversion in TRELLIS but not in 2D diffusion/flow models (FLUX, Stable Diffusion), reinforcing the paper's core claim of a 3D-specific phenomenon.

Favorable comparisons against relevant recent baselines (VoxHammer, native TRELLIS second-stage editing) on the DT4D non-rigid shape benchmark, showing both qualitative superiority (geometry-level edits vs. texture-only changes) and large efficiency gains (~20x speedup, no manual masking).

Good transparency about limitations: the paper explicitly shows and discusses failure cases on extreme out-of-distribution poses (Fig. 9), rather than hiding them, and proposes reasonable future directions.
Reasonable reproducibility support: detailed algorithm pseudocode (Alg. 1) and dataset construction details are provided in the supplementary material.
weaknesses: All experiments rely on a single 3D generative backbone (TRELLIS); the newer TRELLIS.2 is excluded on relevance grounds, so it remains unclear whether the 'sink trap' phenomenon and the proposed fix generalize across other native text-to-3D architectures/backbones.

The quantitative editing evaluation is fairly thin: Table 3 reports a single SigLIP alignment score on essentially one dataset/setting, with no user study or additional perceptual/geometric-plausibility metrics to corroborate that edits are semantically faithful and not just superficially well-aligned in embedding space.

No quantitative comparison against other recent text-driven 3D editing approaches referenced in related work (e.g., Nano3D, 3D-Latte), only against VoxHammer and TRELLIS's native pipeline, limiting the breadth of the empirical case for state-of-the-art status.

The 'expressivity mismatch' framing could be partially confounded with standard training-data distribution effects (i.e., certain semantic categories being underrepresented in the text-to-3D training data) rather than a fundamentally distinct decoupling of geometric vs. linguistic capacity; the paper does not fully rule out this alternative explanation.

The frequency/severity of the acknowledged failure mode (edits on geometrically OOD poses, Fig. 9) is not quantified, making it hard to assess how often practitioners would encounter unreliable edits.
Evaluation datasets are modest in scale (80 TRELLIS-generated shapes, 208 DT4D frames from 13 sequences), which somewhat limits the statistical strength of the quantitative claims.

strengths: Identifies and clearly characterizes a novel and important failure mode in native text-to-3D generative models ("sink trap"), where diverse out-of-distribution prompts collapse to near-identical geometries; this is a valuable diagnostic contribution not previously documented in the 3D generative modeling literature.

The diversity-ratio metric (Δvis/Δtxt using SigLIP) is a reasonable and reproducible way to quantify the language-geometry mismatch, and the authors validate the phenomenon across three different 3D generative backbones (TRELLIS, LN3Diff, GaussianAnything), strengthening the generality of the observation.

The proposed fix (empty-prompt Euler inversion + null-text optimization) is simple, well-motivated by the velocity-norm/CFG instability analysis, and is shown to substantially improve reconstruction (L1/LPIPS) over approximate-prompt inversion and over the standard NTI baseline on non-rigid DT4D shapes.

The resulting editing pipeline is compared against multiple strong/relevant baselines (VoxHammer, TRELLIS native second-stage editing, Vox-E, Instant3DiT) with both quantitative (SigLIP/CLIP/VLM scores) and qualitative results, and shows clear advantages in geometric retargeting fidelity while being far more computationally efficient (~9s/edit vs. >1 hour for Vox-E) and mask-free unlike VoxHammer/Instant3DiT.

The paper extends the analysis to 2D T2I models (FLUX, Stable Diffusion, COCO/DiffusionDB) to contrast behavior, providing useful context that the sink-trap instability is comparatively more severe in native 3D generative latent spaces than in mature 2D diffusion models.

Reasonably thorough supplementary material (algorithm pseudocode, dataset construction details, additional qualitative figures) supports reproducibility, and limitations (failure on highly OOD poses, lack of explicit plausibility constraints) are honestly discussed.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is somewhat incremental: it largely amounts to substituting an approximate source prompt with an empty/null prompt within existing Euler inversion + NTI machinery (already established in the 2D domain), rather than a fundamentally new mechanism tailored to 3D flow latents.

The full editing pipeline and quantitative editing evaluations (Table 3, Fig. 7-9) are demonstrated only on TRELLIS; the multi-model generality claim is supported only by the diversity-ratio analysis (Table 1) for LN3Diff and GaussianAnything, not by the actual inversion/editing experiments, leaving open whether the proposed fix generalizes to other backbones.

VLM-based evaluation relies on LLaVA-1.5-7B, a relatively dated and weaker VLM by current standards, which may add noise or bias to the reported editing-quality scores; no human study or stronger/more recent VLM judge is used to corroborate results.

Structural fidelity is not guaranteed: as acknowledged in Fig. 9 and the limitations section, edits on rare/OOD poses can produce implausible geometries since the method does not explicitly enforce geometric plausibility, somewhat undercutting the robustness claims made elsewhere in the paper.

Some comparisons are qualitative only or explicitly excluded from quantitative tables (e.g., "3D-latte" is mentioned in related work but not benchmarked; full-scene editing methods are excluded from Table 3 "for fairness"), which narrows the empirical comparison set and could understate the competitiveness of alternative approaches.

The efficiency claim (~9s per edit) is stated without full detail on how NTI's 10 inner optimization steps over 50 timesteps achieves this speed, and hardware/timing methodology could be more explicitly documented for reproducibility.

strengths: Identifies and empirically documents an interesting and previously under-explored failure mode ('sink trap') in native text-to-3D flow models, where text conditioning becomes insensitive to prompt variation for certain semantic categories, while the model's unconditional geometric prior remains expressive.

The proposed fix -- inverting with an empty/null prompt combined with null-text-style optimization of unconditional embeddings, then editing purely via the target prompt -- is simple, is shown to work across several qualitative examples, and requires no auxiliary masks, 2D inpainting models, or image priors, unlike most existing 3D editing pipelines.

Reasonably broad empirical support: the diversity/sink-trap analysis (SigLIP-based R ratio) is shown on three different 3D generative backbones (TRELLIS, LN3Diff, GaussianAnything), and the inversion-stability analysis is cross-checked against 2D T2I baselines (FLUX, Stable Diffusion) and additional COCO/DiffusionDB experiments, lending some generality to the core diagnosis.

Reasonably thorough ablations comparing Euler vs. NTI inversion under true/approximate/empty prompts (Tables 2 and 4), and quantitative + qualitative comparisons against relevant recent 3D-editing baselines (VoxHammer, Vox-E, Instant3DiT, TRELLIS native edit).

Practical efficiency advantage over per-scene SDS-style optimization (Vox-E) and masking-heavy pipelines (VoxHammer, Instant3DiT), reportedly needing only voxelization and a few generative passes per edit.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core technical contribution is largely a direct adaptation of Null-Text Inversion (an established 2D technique) combined with the well-known trick of using an empty/null conditioning prompt, applied to the TRELLIS 3D latent space. The paper's main new element is the diagnostic framing ('sink trap') rather than a new algorithmic mechanism.

The full editing pipeline (Sec. 4.3, 5.3, main figures) is evaluated almost exclusively on a single 3D backbone (TRELLIS); the multi-backbone analysis (LN3Diff, GaussianAnything) is restricted to the diversity/R-ratio diagnostic in Sec. 4.1 and not carried through to the proposed editing method, which weakens claims of general applicability across 'text-to-3D generative models.'

No human evaluation is conducted despite editing quality being fundamentally about semantic correctness and geometric plausibility; the VLM-based scoring relies on LLaVA-1.5-7B, a comparatively dated and weaker vision-language model, whose 1-5 rubric reliability is not validated (e.g., via correlation with human judgments or a stronger/more recent VLM).

The claim that the diversity ratio R is 'closely related to the Lipschitz constant' is asserted rather than formally derived or justified, and the paper itself notes cosine distance does not define a metric space, undermining the rigor of this framing.

Fig. 9 and the Limitations section show that edits on rare/OOD poses still produce implausible geometries, indicating the proposed fix does not fully resolve the underlying sink-trap/OOD problem it diagnoses, and no quantitative failure-rate analysis is given for how often this occurs.

The 'geometric expressivity' argument (Sec 4.3) is somewhat circular: showing that null-text-optimized inversion with an empty prompt can reconstruct an arbitrary target shape is close to a curve-fitting result (optimizing unconditional embeddings against a reference latent), and the paper does not sufficiently disentangle how much of the subsequent edit's semantic fidelity comes from the model's generative prior versus the optimization's tendency to preserve/overfit the source structure.

Editing evaluation is conducted only on the first-stage structure latent (G_S) with the second-stage refinement (G_L) kept fixed/seeded; the paper acknowledges modifying G_L yields only texture-level changes, but it is unclear how much this design choice limits final asset quality/texture-geometry consistency in the actual rendered results shown in the figures.

Baseline comparison fairness is questionable in places: VoxHammer reportedly fails on 67% of DT4D samples due to latent value explosion, which is attributed to the baseline rather than examined for whether preprocessing/dataset selection disadvantages it.

Minor writing/clarity issues (e.g., grammatical errors in figure captions such as 'overall geometry overall sample') and some figures (e.g., Fig. 6 edit prompts) are only partially specified in the main text, requiring cross-referencing to supplementary JSON files for full reproducibility.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly characterized 'sink trap' phenomenon: the paper provides a compelling quantitative (SigLIP-based diversity ratio R) and qualitative (Fig. 2, Table 1) demonstration that text-to-3D models like TRELLIS, LN3Diff, and GaussianAnything collapse to near-identical geometries for out-of-distribution prompts, despite retaining the geometric capacity to represent diverse shapes.

The core insight—that combining an empty/null conditioning prompt with null-text optimization stabilizes inversion trajectories and unlocks the model's unconditional geometric prior—is simple, well-supported by velocity-norm analysis (Fig. 4), and effectively decouples geometric expressivity from linguistic sensitivity, a genuinely useful diagnostic and practical fix.

Strong empirical validation across multiple axes: reconstruction quality (L1, LPIPS) comparisons across prompt types and inversion methods (Table 2, Table 4), downstream editing quality via SigLIP/CLIP/VLM scores against several strong baselines (VoxHammer, Vox-E, Instant3DiT, native TRELLIS editing) with consistent improvements (Table 3), and cross-domain confirmation that the same prompt-insensitivity trend is much weaker in 2D T2I models (FLUX, SD) via matched experiments (Sec. F, Table 5), which strengthens the causal story that this is a 3D-specific issue.

Practical advantages are demonstrated, including large efficiency gains (~9s/edit) over slower baselines (Vox-E >1hr, VoxHammer needing manual masks and 150+ rendered views), and multiview-consistent 3D-native edits (Fig. 8) without requiring 2D priors, masks, or auxiliary image-based guidance—addressing a real gap identified in related work.

Honest limitations section (Fig. 9) showing failure cases on highly out-of-distribution poses, plus a thorough supplementary material with algorithm pseudocode (Alg. 1), dataset preparation details, and extensive additional qualitative results supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The method and empirical validation are anchored almost entirely to TRELLIS's first-stage sparse structure model; the second-stage refinement (texture/SLAT) is kept fixed throughout, and no experiments generalize the full editing pipeline to other 3D generative backbones (LN3Diff/GaussianAnything are used only for the diversity analysis, not for editing/inversion validation), leaving open how well the proposed inversion+editing recipe transfers beyond one architecture.

Editing quality evaluation relies substantially on automatic proxies (SigLIP/CLIP similarity, LLaVA-1.5-7B scoring with a self-defined 1-5 rubric) without a human user study, which is a comparatively weak evidence source for subjective notions like editing plausibility and prompt fidelity.

The comparison with VoxHammer may be somewhat imbalanced: it fails on 67% of DT4D samples due to latent-value explosion, and it also requires manual 3D masks, which are structurally different requirements than the proposed method's; while the paper appropriately notes these differences, the quantitative gap partly reflects this mismatch rather than a purely like-for-like editing-quality comparison.

The diversity ratio R (Sec. 4.1) is a useful heuristic but is based on cosine similarity in a non-metric embedding space and is not validated against any ground-truth notion of geometric diversity (e.g., correlation with human judgments or explicit shape-space distances), so its precision as a measure of 'sink trap' severity is somewhat informal.

Failure cases (Fig. 9) are shown only qualitatively; there is no quantitative characterization of how often or under what conditions the editing pipeline becomes unstable for rare/OOD poses, which would help readers gauge the practical reliability of the method.

The computational cost accounting (9s/edit) is not clearly broken out to include the null-text inversion cost (50 steps × 10 inner Adam iterations), which could be a substantial overhead not fully reflected in the reported efficiency comparison.
